excerpt.rendered: How Southeast Asia’s famously pungent fruit became a source of cultural identity and global demand.

content.rendered:
In 2019, 550 students evacuated the University of Canberra’s library because of one fruit: durian. Its sulfuric odor had been mistaken for a gas leak, a common occurrence that has grounded planes and baffled fire departments worldwide. Known colloquially as the “King of the Fruits,” durian commands attention with its pungent scent and spiky husk. Despite these seemingly unsavory qualities, durian’s sweet flesh has created a multibillion-dollar consumer market that fuels economic growth in countries like Vietnam, Malaysia, Cambodia, and Thailand. Central to Southeast Asia’s ecological systems, economic development, and sociopolitical organization, durian’s overpowering presence shapes local customs and mobilizes transnational supply chains, testifying to the sensorial hold that plants have over us.

For those unacquainted with the peculiar odor, taste, and texture of durian, American botanist Francis Ramaley’s 1905 account offers a helpful starting point. He describes durian’s smell as a “rare combination of vile odors”: “first one thinks of rotten eggs, then of sewer gas and garlic and finally he gives up any attempt at a classification of the different smells.” By contrast, in one of the most vehement defenses of the fruit, British naturalist and “confirmed Durian eater” Alfred Russel Wallace waxes lyrical in his 1869 travelogue The Malay Archipelago:

A rich butter-like custard highly flavoured with almonds gives the best general idea of it, but intermingled with it come wafts of flavour that call to mind cream-cheese, onion-sauce, brown sherry, and other incongruities. Then there is a rich glutinous smoothness in the pulp which nothing else possesses, but which adds to its delicacy. It is neither acid, nor sweet, nor juicy; yet one feels the want of none of these qualities, for it is perfect as it is. […] In fact to eat Durians is a new sensation, worth a voyage to the East to experience.

These contrasting colonial accounts show that durian was just as polarizing then as it is today. More importantly, Ramaley and Wallace both recognized durian’s powerful effect on the senses and the intensely visceral responses it evoked, whether expressed in terms of disgust or desire. It is precisely this complexity and intensity that characterizes durian, a fruit whose importance in Southeast Asia goes beyond simple binaries like the detestable and the delightful, the economic and the cultural, or the local and the transnational.

Although the Durio genus has more than 28 recognized species, durian (Durio zibethinus) is the most commonly cultivated species for human consumption. At least 200 cultivars have been developed through human selection, and the plant has spread from its native Borneo, Sumatra, and Peninsular Malaysia to Thailand, Cambodia, and Vietnam. The characteristic smell of durian has been attributed to a combination of many different scent molecules, but scientists still struggle to pin down the exact compounds responsible, even with advanced chemical analysis techniques. The strong notes of fruity esters and sulphurous compounds are thought to serve as an important biological mechanism for attracting animals to consume the fruit and disperse its seeds.

There is a Balinese saying: “Buka durene hulung, masih ada ngaput,” which translates to “As with a fallen durian, there is someone who picks it up.”

Still, wild durians are relatively scarce because the fruit’s large seeds, tough husks, and thorny exterior mean that only large terrestrial mammals like elephants and macaques can participate in its seed dispersal

title.rendered: Can We Recover a Worldview Lost to Colonialism?

excerpt.rendered: Among the Ao Naga of northeast India, humans may have been just one kind of person in a world filled with spiritual beings.

content.rendered:
How did people see the world before older systems were displaced by colonialism? This is a question faced by communities all over the world. Anthropologist Tiatemsu Longkumer considers it in regard to one particular group of people, the Ao Naga of northeast India.

Today, Longkumer writes, nearly all Aos are Christian, and none practice the community’s pre-colonial spiritual traditions. And because the Ao Naga did not keep written records before the nineteenth century, written sources can’t tell us how they understood the world.

In contrast to a binary of good and evil, tsüngrem, mojing, and temenen were all understood as entities capable of positive or negative action toward humans.

The earliest written records of the society were created by colonial administrators and Christian missionaries. One such account is “The Ao Naga Tribe of Assam,” written by American sociologist and Baptist missionary W. C. Smith in 1925. Smith described the society as an example of “primitive man” and argued that their worship was driven by a fear of “unknown powers.” He distinguished good spirits known as tsüngrem from bad ones called mojing and temenen.

The following year, British administrator and anthropologist J. P. Mills published “The Ao Nagas,” in which he argued that the Ao religion was not a system of moral rules but instead a set of ceremonies calling on “deities” for help. He laid out a system of supernatural presences, defining “Lichaba” as the godlike chief of tsüngrem.

Since Smith and Mills’ time, Ao Naga Christian theologians have become the foremost experts on their community’s pre-Christian religion. Because these scholars work within a Christian framework, Longkumer writes, they are mainly interested in traditional beliefs and practices as precursors to the full divine revelation represented by the community’s conversion to Christianity.

More to Explore

The Changing Meaning of “Mysticism”

Livia Gershon
August 24, 2021
People who don't follow organized religion sometimes describe themselves as spiritual. But this idea isn't a recent invention.

In an effort to reconstruct what Ao Naga beliefs looked like before they were refracted through Christianity, Longkumer turns to animism, a broad term for worldviews in which humans are just one kind of “person,” with the capacity to be in relation to other entities, including the spirits of rivers and mountains.

Longkumer suggests that Mills’s distinction between morality and ceremony confused the reality of Ao practices, which emphasized the ethical practice of living in harmony with the spiritual world. He argues that Lichaba, an anthropomorphic spirit, should be viewed as just one among many tsüngrem, and that—in contrast to a binary of good and evil—tsüngrem, mojing, and temenen were all understood as entities capable of positive or negative action toward humans.

excerpt.rendered: What gets lost when spoken conversations become part of the historical record?

content.rendered:
Talk-talk, said Winston Churchill (reputedly), is always better than war-war. But how is such diplomatic talk-talk recorded for posterity? Until relatively recently, history has depended mostly on written records. Those are never the same as conversations, which by their very nature are ephemeral. The recollection, reconstruction, and/or condensing, in the “minutes” of a meeting, of what was said is the issue sociologist David R. Gibson explores.

Converting “talk with all its complexities, disfluencies, ambiguities, and occasional disarray, into a written record of who said what,” writes Gibson, is no easy task. Every historian should be aware of the potential pitfalls of this fraught form of translation. And not just historians. With so much of the news reliant on anonymous sources, the issues raised are important for a functioning democracy as well.

“We might say that minutes are not merely taken, but actively made, and the minute-takers are equally minute-makers, sometimes with input from others.”

Meeting minutes, writes Gibson, are “traces of words uttered behind closed doors, but they often have the appearance of a verbatim report, and even when they do not, it is tempting to read them that way, lulling us into erroneous conclusions about who said what, how they said it, and whom they were in agreement with.” Such minutes in the official compendium of “major U.S. foreign policy decisions and significant diplomatic activity” that is the State Department’s Foreign Relations of the United States (FRUS) series are given the imprimatur of history. But what exactly are they? (FRUS holdings begin with the Lincoln administration and are amply voluminous; there are, for instance, 25 volumes for the Kennedy administration and a planned 48 volumes for the Clinton administration.)

Minutes may be edited after the fact, by “the minute-taker or someone else,” notes Gibson. Members of the Soviet Union’s Politburo were neither the first nor the last who could and would alter minutes before they were disseminated. Gibson continues that “we might say that minutes are not merely taken, but actively made, and the minute-takers are equally minute-makers, sometimes with input from others.”

“Memories of talk” in after-the-fact minutes are as suspect as any other memories. “One problem with such recollections is that our ‘conversational memory’ is not especially good,” writes Gibson. “Experimental evidence suggests that we forget much of what was said in a matter of minutes. Another problem is spin.”

More to Explore

The President and the Press Corps

Jordan Friedman
November 6, 2025
Theodore Roosevelt was the first White House occupant to seek control over how newspapers covered him.

Spin, like gravity, seems to be a given. Gibson gives the example of Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy, who “exaggerated his importance as an advocate for the temperate approach that brought the crisis to a peaceful resolution” during the heady days of the Cuban Missile Crisis in October 1962.

The reason we know this is that Kennedy’s brother, President John F. Kennedy, was secretly taping those National Security Council Executive Committee meetings in which the launch of World War III was seriously contemplated. So there is something to compare RFK’s retelling to.

The advent of relatively cheap audio recording in the second half of the last century began to allow for such comparisons of taped recordings with written records. They can be like night and day. British parliamentary proceedings, as one example, were taken by shorthand-reporters working five–ten-minute shifts. Recordings show these reporters corrected informal language and grammar, and omitted disfluencies (repetitions, non-lexical vocal sounds, all the “ums/ahs/likes” of actual conversation), making everyone sound a lot better, more, you might say, like, uh, statespersons. Another example, of a police interrogation transcript and audio recording of the same interrogation, showed how the transcript simply skipped over the police officers’ effort to cut a deal with the defendant by incorrectly noting that those passages were “unintelligible.”
